item.title: Smoothing splines with some discontinuities
item.description: arXiv:2610.33137v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We generalize cubic smoothing splines to signals with a finite number of discontinuities at unknown positions. Rather than changing the roughness penalty, we deform the domain over which it is computed: every interval between consecutive observations can be stretched by a non-negative warp, subject to a total budget, and the optimizer spends the budget only where a jump makes stretching cheaper than bending. The estimator inherits the state-space form of smoothing splines, so it can be fitted by maximum likelihood with the Kalman filter, and it also admits a fast alternating algorithm that solves a banded linear system and takes a projected-gradient step on the warps. The budget is selected by an extended Bayesian information criterion whose constant is calibrated by simulation. In a Monte Carlo comparison the new estimators reconstruct a piecewise-smooth signal more accurately than the cubic smoothing spline with discontinuities of Storath and Weinmann, at the cost of more false alarms. Two energy applications illustrate the method: the temperature response of electricity demand in Northern Italy, and retail fuel prices, whose discontinuities, changes in excise duties, are dated by public record. The three supplements follow the references.
item.dc:creator: Matteo Pelagatti (University of Milano-Bicca, Italy), Paolo Maranzano (University of Milano-Bicca, Italy,Fondazione Eni Enrico Mattei, Italy), Giulio Cesare Gatto Ronchieri (University of Milano-Bicca, Italy)

item.title: Self-thresholding angular-radial models of extremal dependence
item.description: arXiv:2610.33238v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Assessing compound risks requires a model for routine and extreme joint behaviour together, and a principled answer to where the joint tail begins. We propose the self-thresholding angular-radial (STAR) model: after marginal standardization, the radius given the angle follows a spliced distribution, with a flexible body below an angle-dependent threshold curve and a generalized Pareto tail above it. The threshold curve is estimated with all other parameters, so its uncertainty propagates to every summary, and the joint density is in closed form because the splice normalizes in one dimension for every angle. The tail scale function is the reciprocal gauge of the implied limit set, and the coefficient of extremal association is an explicit parameter, so a prior with atoms at tail independence and at the asymptotic dependence boundary yields posterior probabilities of the dependence class. At that boundary the copula of the model is asymptotically dependent, while its margins and joint tail are both lighter than exponential by a factor inversely proportional to the level. Simulations show accurate recovery of finite-level dependence summaries within and beyond the model class, and the slow separation of asymptotic dependence from strong asymptotic independence that the theory predicts. For warm-season daily maxima of fine particulate matter and ozone at a Beijing station, the pair is asymptotically independent with posterior probability 0.96 and both pollutants exceed their 0.9 quantiles on about two and a half days per season; the model gives summaries comparable to those of existing approaches without requiring the arbitrary choice of a threshold. The construction extends to d dimensions through pairwise deficits of the gauge, illustrated by adding coarse particulate matter as a third pollutant.
item.dc:creator: Manuele Leonelli, Dani Gamerman

item.title: Informative inference on the average treatment effect with instrumental variables
item.description: arXiv:2610.33254v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Policy decisions often depend on whether the average treatment effect (ATE) exceeds a specific cutoff. In instrumental variable (IV) settings, point identification of the ATE requires strong assumptions that are often difficult to justify. Therefore, many researchers shift their attention to identification of the local (L) ATE or target bounds of the ATE. Both strategies have well-known drawbacks: the substantive relevance of the LATE is frequently questioned, and the bounds are often too wide to be informative. We propose a simple sensitivity analysis that allows researchers to maintain focus on the ATE, and then discuss its connection to related bounding procedures. Based on these results, researchers can decide, in a principled manner, whether the sign of the ATE is inferable under assumptions they deem credible. The proposed strategies are easy to apply, and we illustrate their value with two real-data examples. The R package ivate implements our procedures.
item.dc:creator: Luca Locher, Thomas Richardson, Mats Stensrud

item.title: Not All Mislabels Are Equal: Efficient Task-Aware Auditing with Confidence Sequences
item.description: arXiv:2610.33262v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study efficient, adaptive auditing of categorical labels in a fixed dataset, motivated by biodiversity-credit programs in which expert verification of species records is costly and downstream scores (e.g., payment) are more sensitive to errors on certain labels than on others. Our proposed ATLAS framework couples anytime-valid inference with a task-aware adaptive auditing policy. Representing label corrections through a confusion matrix, we prioritize which data points to inspect next based on both label uncertainty and the influence of potential label corrections on the downstream score function. For linear scores such as the mislabel rate, our priority-aware approach certifies the overall label error rate to $\pm 2$ percentage points with 24% and 11% fewer audits than random sampling on biodiversity data from Kenya and a widely used CIFAR-10N benchmark, respectively. For nonlinear scores such as the Hill-Shannon diversity, we exploit a linear-envelope representation that reduces inference to a family of linear-score audits; priority-aware sampling reaches the target precision with 36% fewer audits. When distribution-free guarantees are prohibitively costly, we develop a model-based Bayesian alternative that trades assumption-free validity for substantially fewer audits. Our biodiversity case study highlights a gap between statistical validity and practical feasibility: generic methods such as Serfling's bound and existing confidence-sequence procedures are rigorous but can require prohibitively many expert reviews in practice. Together, these results show task-aware auditing can significantly reduce the number of expert audits needed while providing finite-sample, anytime-valid guarantees.
item.dc:creator: Fangyuan Lin, Noah Krever, Jakub \v{C}ern\'y, Lily Xu

item.title: Robust bootstrap methods for meta-analyses of diagnostic test accuracy studies
item.description: arXiv:2610.33270v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Meta-analysis of diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) commonly relies on the bivariate linear mixed model (BLMM) and the bivariate generalized linear mixed model (BGLMM) to jointly synthesize diagnostic test sensitivity (Se) and specificity (Sp). However, reliance on asymptotic theory and random-effects distributional assumptions may affect finite-sample inference, particularly in small meta-analyses or when the random effects are non-normal. We proposed three bootstrap-based approaches: a nonparametric bootstrap (NPB), a parametric bootstrap (PB), and a bias-corrected parametric bootstrap (BCPB), with the latter two based on a fitted BGLMM. NPB model parameters were estimated using inverse-variance-covariance weighted least squares. Extensive simulations under bivariate normal, Student-t, and Laplace random-effects distributions evaluated finite-sample performance and robustness to departures from normality. Results were qualitatively similar across the three distributions. The bootstrap approaches generally outperformed BLMM in terms of bias, root mean squared error (RMSE), and coverage probability, particularly when diagnostic accuracy is high and the number of studies is small. The BCPB demonstrated the strongest finite-sample performance among the bootstrap approaches, frequently achieving the lowest bias and RMSE for pooled sensitivity and specificity while maintaining coverage probabilities close to the nominal level. The BGLMM also performed well across most settings. The NPB approach generally improved upon the BLMM while providing a flexible alternative without parametric random-effects assumptions. Real-data applications further illustrated the practical utility of the proposed approaches. Overall, the bootstrap methods provide useful alternatives for DTA meta-analysis, particularly when the number of studies is small or random-effects distributional assumptions are uncertain.
item.dc:creator: Diribsa T. Bedada, Olana A. Dabi, Isaac Fordjour, Zelalem F. Negeri

item.title: The kernel mean embedding of a random probability distribution and its principal components
item.description: arXiv:2610.33286v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given a random probability distribution \(F\), whose realizations are defined on \(\mathbb R^d\), and a kernel \(k\), our aim is to analyze the properties of the kernel mean embedding, \(\mu_F\), of \(F\) as a random element of the corresponding reproducing kernel Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\). This establishes a rigorous framework in which kernel statistical techniques for distributional data can be stated both in the sample and population settings and, thus, the asymptotic properties of sample procedures can be properly established. As an illustration of this approach we focus on the principal components of \(F\). We obtain a general convergence result and the explicit expression of the spectral decomposition for the uncentered covariance operator of a normal probability distribution with a Gaussian distributed expectation. The performance of this kernel principal components procedure is illustrated with simulations and the analysis of the intensity distribution in synthetic aperture radar images.
item.dc:creator: Amparo Ba\'illo, Mart\'in S\'anchez-Signorini

item.title: Recursive moment updates for scalable Bayesian nonparametric regression
item.description: arXiv:2610.33388v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bayesian nonparametric regression methods have wide applications in statistics and machine learning, but inference can often be expensive or require approximations. This paper introduces a class of recursive moment function updates which are closed form, interpretable, expedient, and fully quantify Bayesian uncertainty through the martingale posterior. The proposed recursive updates can be used off-the-shelf and encompass challenging scenarios such as nonparametric heteroscedasticity, heavy-tailed or skewed noise, and importantly generalize to the multi-output case with missing outcomes without any significant loss in tractability or speed. We show frequentist consistency under weak assumptions in the aforementioned scenarios, and demonstrate empirically that our proposed method is orders of magnitude faster than competing Bayesian nonparametric approaches, with competitive or even superior prediction and estimation accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Peter Liu, Andrew Yiu, Edwin Fong

item.title: Fitting time-varying parameter models via partially noncentered parametrizations
item.description: arXiv:2610.33392v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time-varying parameter (TVP) models are widely used to capture evolving relationships but inference is often computationally demanding due to high-dimensional latent states. The efficiency of iterative algorithms depends critically on the choice of latent state augmentation, with centering preferred for genuinely time-varying coefficients and noncentering favored when coefficients are nearly constant. We propose a partially noncentered parametrization that bridges these extremes via dimension-specific working parameters for both location and scale. Optimal working parameters are derived by analyzing EM convergence rates, and an alternating expectation-conditional maximization algorithm is developed to implement the approach. As the convergence rate of mean-field variational Bayes (MFVB) is closely related to EM, we extend the approach to develop partially noncentered MFVB algorithms for the TVP model, placing triple gamma priors on baseline coefficients and process variances to induce shrinkage. Simulations and empirical applications show that the resulting MFVB algorithms yield posterior approximations closer to Markov chain Monte Carlo than conventional centered or noncentered parametrizations. We also develop an efficient solver for the block tridiagonal inverse matrices arising in the proposed algorithms.
item.dc:creator: Lingjie Wang, Rufeng Liu, Abhinek Shukla, Linda S. L. Tan

item.title: Exhaustive adjustment-set selection and causal effects for distribution-valued outcomes, with inference under latent Gaussian spatio-temporal dependence
item.description: arXiv:2610.33395v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Selecting adjustment covariates for a distribution-valued outcome must preserve dependence that scalar summaries can discard, and surveillance outcomes are also dependent across space and time. Under unconfoundedness and a relative-overlap condition we identify average treatment effects, stochastic and incremental intervention effects, and natural direct and indirect effects for such outcomes, with doubly and triply robust scores. For independent data, adjustment sets are selected exhaustively by distance-covariance sufficient dimension reduction: we give a root-n projector expansion, a basis-invariant criterion tensor, and a simultaneous outer confidence collection calibrated by fractional sampling with a finite-population correction. For dependence, units are functions of a latent Gaussian field, exponential in space and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck in time, plus independent noise. Such data are $\rho$-mixing at an exponential rate, and the covariance between any two square-integrable scores is a power series in the latent correlation with positive semidefinite coefficients. Consequences include a central limit theorem for all the causal estimators, the exact undercoverage of independence-based intervals, a consistent Mehler covariance estimator under finite chaos order, and an asymptotically conservative convex-chord estimator; block fractional sampling extends the collection under an assumed linearization. In simulations, fractional sampling raises weak-signal collection coverage from .69-.78 to at least .98 while retaining nearly all candidate sets, and the dependence-aware estimators substantially reduce undercoverage, although none is exact when few units fall within a correlation range. A descriptive analysis of U.S. syphilis surveillance and Medicaid expansion illustrates the estimands and compares dependence-aware with conventional inference.
item.dc:creator: Hsin-Hsiung Huang

item.title: Nonparametric shrinkage estimation of high-dimensional variance component matrices
item.description: arXiv:2610.33431v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a nonparametric spectral estimation method for variance component covariance matrices in high-dimensional multivariate mixed effects models. Although classical MANOVA estimators are unbiased entrywise, their eigenvalues can be severely dispersed and biased when the number of traits is comparable to the number of realizations of the random effects. Building on a system of self-consistent equations that characterizes the limiting spectral distribution of a MANOVA estimator, we construct a kernel-based nonlinear transformation of the sample eigenvalues that targets the optimal rotation-invariant estimator under Frobenius loss. The resulting procedure corrects for high-dimensional eigenvalue spreading without imposing a parametric model on the unknown covariance spectrum. Our work is motivated by applications in quantitative genetics, where estimating genetic covariance components across many phenotypic traits is of central interest. We implement the method in a new Python package mlmm-shrinkage and compare the proposed estimator with classical estimators across several common experimental designs in this domain through simulations and a real-data application.
item.dc:creator: Ran Xie, Iain M. Johnstone

item.title: Causal Inference in Metric Spaces via Distance Profiles
item.description: arXiv:2610.33491v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern interventions increasingly produce object-valued outcomes, such as distributions, covariance matrices, networks, and trees. Existing causal frameworks often exploit special geometry such as one-dimensional Wasserstein quantiles or geodesic Fr\'echet means, whereas metric statistics studies random objects without confounding adjustment. We propose the profile causal effect $\Delta(\omega,t)$, which describes where and at what scale a treatment shifts probability mass, including changes in dispersion, tails, or structure that leave mean-level summaries unchanged. Formally, $\Delta(\omega,t)=\Pr\{d(\omega,Y(1))\le t\}-\Pr\{d(\omega,Y(0))\le t\}$ contrasts the potential-outcome probabilities of the same anchor-centered metric ball and requires no structure beyond the metric. On grids fixed by a deterministic or auxiliary design, we combine cross-fitted doubly robust scores with high-dimensional Gaussian approximation and the multiplier bootstrap to obtain simultaneous confidence bands and a global test under regularity conditions. The bands bound treatment-induced changes in ball and shell probabilities simultaneously and, at fixed anchors, extend to all radii. A protocol guides the choice of anchors and radii. Across the experiments, the global test detects concentration effects that mean-quantile and Fr\'echet-mean summaries miss. Its empirical size is near or below the nominal level, even under confounding, where naive metric tests are substantially oversized.
item.dc:creator: Zheye Song, Zhiheng Zhang

item.title: From Average Effects to Proportions Benefiting: A Tutorial on ETZ-Powered Counterfactual Individual Benefit Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.33600v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Consider the question: "Is it true that at least 80% of patients would benefit more from receiving a new treatment, $Rx$, than from receiving a standard treatment, $C$?" Conventional treatment efficacy analyses based on average treatment effects cannot directly answer this question. Yet, even if the true mean treatment effects were known exactly, the answer to this question could still be either "yes" or "no", depending on the variability in patients' treatment responses and the dependence between their potential outcomes. This tutorial introduces a proportion-based perspective on individualized treatment benefit through the ETZ-powered Counterfactual Individual Benefit Analysis framework. We present two metrics, the individual benefit probability and the individual benefit lower bound, which enable confidence-based assessments of whether a prespecified proportion of patients achieves a clinically meaningful treatment benefit. We develop these metrics in both the factual random-pair and counterfactual same-patient settings. In particular, the ETZ decomposition provides a transparent characterization of different sources of outcome variability and enables more precise uncertainty quantification for counterfactual treatment comparisons. We illustrate the framework and its practical implementation using patient-level data from a Phase II randomized clinical trial. By shifting the focus from average treatment effects to population proportions of individual benefit, this tutorial provides a complementary perspective for evaluating treatment efficacy and informing individualized treatment decisions while controlling the type I error rate at a prespecified level.
item.dc:creator: Xingya Wang, Yang Han, Yushi Liu, Szu-Yu Tang, Jason C. Hsu

item.title: Identification and curvature bias for shared inputs in multichannel dynamical models
item.description: arXiv:2610.33642v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pooling many channels with a shared unknown input can leave persistent bias when each channel retains a fixed number of observations and its own incidental parameters. For heterogeneous smooth channel manifolds under isotropic noise, the second-order bias is an information-weighted regression of mean curvature on normal input velocity. A feasible correction gives centred Gaussian inference as the noise level $\sigma$ decreases with $R\sigma^6\to0$, compared with $R\sigma^2\to0$ without correction. We extend the stochastic expansion and studentization to deterministic channel arrays with densely correlated Gaussian errors of bounded covariance operator norm. General marginal covariance adds a forcing term that can bias even flat channels, while cross-channel covariance changes uncertainty. For Gaussian errors with a separable frame-by-channel covariance whose channel factor is autoregressive in a known ordering, an independent zero-mean calibration field yields a covariance estimator accurate enough for corrected inference. Boundary accumulation and fixed working population models introduce distinct bias terms; rational-multiplier and zero-count arguments connect identification to frame-integrated compartment models. Simulations test both oracle and estimated-covariance inference, including independent PET replications. Moderate-noise undercoverage, optimization ambiguity and the need to validate reconstruction covariance limit practical inference. The real-data example supports sensitivity analysis, not clinically calibrated intervals.
item.dc:creator: Hsin-Hsiung Huang

item.title: Renewable model averaging for generalized linear models
item.description: arXiv:2610.33665v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prediction is one of the most important research topics in statistics and machine learning. Moreover, in the domain of streaming data analysis, real-time prediction has become a rapidly growing research field in recent years, owing to the abundance of streaming data. In many fields of scientific research, such as biomedical research, weather forecasting, and traffic management, improving real-time prediction of streaming data is crucial in general. However, the complicated features of streaming data, such as large-scale and high-velocity, impose both theoretical and computational challenges to the development and evaluation of real-time prediction in this field, especially when the investigator has multiple models at hand. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel Renewable Model Averaging method through Quadratic approximation (ReMAQ) for generalized linear model (GLM) for streaming data. By approximating the model averaging procedure for GLMs (which is typically a convex optimization problem) with a quadratic optimization formulation, ReMAQ allows us to update the model averaging prediction sequentially when a new batch of data arrives, without accessing the entire historical data. Moreover, ReMAQ is also computationally efficient as one only needs to consider a quadratic programming problem in each steps of updating. Under certain regular conditions, we also show that the proposed ReMAQ weight is asymptotically equivalent to that by the oracle model averaging based on the inaccessible full data, the asymptotic optimality of ReMAQ is then established accordingly. The proposed method is also assessed by simulation studies. We apply our proposed ReMAQ in the study of the Airline On-Time Performance Dataset and the results demonstrate the superiority our method in practical situations.
item.dc:creator: Yalu Ping, Chen Xuerong, Yu Dalei

item.title: SoftBART-CORM Models for Density Regression
item.description: arXiv:2610.33669v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Flexible modelling of the conditional distribution of a response given predictors is important in many applications where nonlinear effects, heteroskedasticity, and multimodality may be present. We introduce the SoftBART-CoRM, a predictor-dependent infinite mixture model that combines the interpretable component structure of Compound Random Measures (CoRMs) with SoftBART priors on both mixture weights and component-specific parameters. The model flexibly captures complex distributional features, while global--local shrinkage and predictor-selection priors mitigate overfitting and identify the covariates driving component allocation and kernel parameters. Posterior inference is performed using an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm that leverages existing \texttt{R} implementations of SoftBART. Through simulation studies and real-data applications, we show that the proposed approach can adaptively shrink towards simpler mixture representations, provide interpretable inference on the predictors governing different aspects of the conditional distribution, and achieve superior out-of-sample predictive performance relative to benchmark models.
item.dc:creator: Jim E. Griffin, Maria Kalli

item.title: An Integrated Framework for Assessing Interpretability in Exploratory Factor Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.33670v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interpretability in Exploratory Factor Analysis is characterized by the fundamental trade-off between structural sparseness and explained common variance. Lacking formal evaluation metrics, researchers frequently sacrifice parsimony in the pattern matrix to maximize the model's explanatory coverage. For this reason, we extend Hoyer's sparseness ratio into a flexible \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal{L}_{p_1}/\mathcal{L}_{p_2}$}{Lp1/Lp2} formulation to introduce the Interpretability Index $I$, defined as the geometric mean of explained common variance and the generalized sparseness index. We analyze the asymptotic behavior of $I$ as norm orders increase, establishing that raising $p_2$ alone yields a stable limit, whereas increasing $p_1$ and $p_2$ jointly causes the measure to saturate. The canonical choice $(p_1,p_2)=(2,4)$ balances numerical stability with a smooth, tractable objective. We finally demonstrate, on five benchmark datasets from the statistical literature, how the Interpretability Index provides a systematic criterion for selecting the optimal parametrization of the latent space according to the user's analytical goals.
item.dc:creator: Mariaelena Bottazzi Schenone, Tiziano Iannaccio, Ilaria Mozzetta, Maurizio Vichi

item.title: Estimating Stability of Individual-Specific Predictions from AI-based prediction models using Bootstrap and Cross-validation Resampling
item.description: arXiv:2610.33744v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clinical prediction models are typically developed in a single finite dataset, which is one of many possible datasets that could have been collected. Applying the same model development procedure in another sample will provide different predictions for an individual. The degree to which an individual's prediction varies across development sets is referred to as prediction instability and is not captured by average performance measures. Resampling of the training data offers a practical way to assess instability, but its ability to do so accurately and reliably for different model choices is unclear. In a simulation study, we considered non-parametric, parametric, and out-of-bag bootstrap methods and repeated 10-, 5-, and 2-fold cross-validation (CV) to estimate metrics of prediction instability for Elastic Net logistic regression and Random Forest. The same metrics estimated in independent development samples provided the reference. We assessed individual-level prediction variance, empirical 95% range width, and mean absolute differences from the original prediction and true outcome probability. Instability increased in smaller development samples, was greater for Random Forest, and varied across the probability range. Repeated 5- and 10-fold CV underestimated prediction instability across scenarios. Default non-parametric bootstrap more closely approximated independent sampling for Elastic Net but often overestimated instability for Random Forest, as did parametric bootstrap. Out-of-bag bootstrap and repeated 2-fold CV generally agreed most closely with independent sampling, although no procedure was uniformly best. Resampling procedures should not be used interchangeably, nor should less variable predictions be taken as evidence of greater stability. To estimate prediction instability, prefer procedures that predict on held-out data and limit overlap between training resamples.
item.dc:creator: Alex Carriero, Martijn L. G. van Dam, Anne A. H. de Hond, Richard D. Riley, Gary S. Collins, Karel G. M. Moons, Maarten van Smeden, Nicole S. Erler

item.title: AI-assisted design and analysis of experiments with unstructured treatments
item.description: arXiv:2610.33818v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Randomized experiments involving complex, unstructured treatments such as text, images, or video, are increasingly common in social science research. The goal of many of these studies is to estimate the effect of a structured, interpretable attribute that generalizes beyond the treatments used in the experiment (e.g., the presence of a linguistic or visual feature). There are two key challenges when conducting such studies: observed effects of the attribute of interest (i) may be confounded by other correlated attributes, leading to poor internal validity; and (ii) may not generalize beyond the treatments used in the experiment, leading to poor external validity. We propose a framework for designing experiments with unstructured treatments that leverages generative AI or large databases to sample treatments in a way that explicitly navigates the tradeoff between internal and external validity. We show how to conduct conservative asymptotic inference with a difference-in-means estimator, and develop a calibrated AI-assisted estimator that incorporates zero-shot AI predictions to improve precision without introducing bias. Throughout, we work in a finite population framework, where treatment assignment is the only source of randomness, and treat AI generations and predictions as black-boxes with no guarantees on their performance. We illustrate and evaluate our approach by designing two hypothetical experiments, one with text and another with images.
item.dc:creator: Eli Ben-Michael, Zach Branson

item.title: Optimal Experimental Design for the Polynomial Maximization Method: a Higher-Order Reserve Beyond Second-Order Design Theory
item.description: arXiv:2610.33921v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optimal designs for regression with asymmetric errors build on the second-order least squares estimator (SLSE) of Wang and Leblanc (2008), whose gain over ordinary least squares (OLS) comes from the error skewness. With i.i.d. errors the optimally weighted SLSE solves the same estimating equation as the degree-two Polynomial Maximization Method (PMM), a family whose degree-$S$ location estimator has asymptotic variance $g_S\le1$ times that of the sample mean. We derive optimal designs for this family when the errors are independent with constant variance but have standardised cumulants of order three and higher that vary with the regressor (cumulant heteroscedasticity). For a known reduction field $g_S(x)$, the $g_S$-weighted information matrix $M_{g_S}$ obeys the Kiefer-Wolfowitz equivalence theorem. A constant field leaves the OLS-optimal design unchanged; a non-constant field can change it but need not. For symmetric errors with varying kurtosis, the PMM$_2$ and conditional-SLSE designs cannot depart from the OLS-optimal one, whereas a degree-three design can. A stratify-and-pool PMM$_S$ estimator attains $N\mathrm{Cov}(\hat\theta)\to\sigma^2M_{g_S}^{-1}$ at every degree as all strata grow; its per-stratum reduction is below one only for symmetric errors with the symmetry imposed. For a quadratic model on $[0,1]$ with symmetric Beta errors of unit variance and dose-varying shape, the third-order design for the known field has $A$-efficiency $1.047$ relative to the OLS-optimal design, and $1.001$ under the $D$-criterion. A two-stage procedure that estimates the field from a one-third pilot builds designs of $A$-efficiency $1.014$-$1.020$ at $N=600$-$2400$; its realised mean-squared-error ratio against the OLS-optimal design ranges from $0.89$ (a loss) to $1.08$.
item.dc:creator: Serhii Zabolotnii

item.title: On the Consistency of Spectral Clustering under Generalized Gaussian Mixture Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.33944v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spectral clustering is a widely used clustering method with strong empirical performance and favorable computational scalability. Existing theory has established its consistency and risk guarantees under Gaussian and related mixture models, primarily in settings with relatively simple latent structure. In this paper, we study spectral clustering under a semiparametric Gaussian mixture model, where the observed data become Gaussian-mixture distributed only after unknown monotone coordinate-wise transformations. We derive non-asymptotic bounds for its cluster recovery error. As a byproduct of the theory, we show that spectral clustering provides a theoretically justified initialization for a broad class of high-dimensional mixture-based learning procedures.
item.dc:creator: Lyuou Zhang, Boxiang Wang, Wen Zhou, Hui Zou

item.title: Extreme proxies for causal identification: deconfounding with outliers
item.description: arXiv:2610.34002v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Causal identification under unobserved confounding typically relies on additional structure, such as a valid instrument or proxy variables. We show that heavy tailed variables offer an alternative route to identification by revealing treatment variation for which confounding becomes asymptotically negligible. Our key assumption is extreme propagation: when an unobserved confounder takes an extreme value, some observed variable in the system (called a safeguard) will become extreme with large probability. This way, selecting extreme treatment observations while safeguards remain non-extreme makes confounding asymptotically negligible relative to the treatment. We call this certification. We derive graphical conditions specifying which latent confounders must be monitored by safeguards and distributional conditions ensuring effective certification. The framework includes valid-instrument and double-proxy structures as special cases, as well as confounded instruments that are invalid in most approaches that do not exploit heavy tails. Geometrically, certification isolates the extremal ray whose slope equals the causal effect. This connects causal identification with multivariate extreme-value geometry and motivates a family of novel simple estimators. Simulations demonstrate performance gains under nonlinear confounding and heavy tails, while revealing limitations in light-tailed regimes (where cancellation can conceal extreme confounding from the safeguards). We validate our methodology in simulation studies and by recovering the ground-truth flow in a river discharge application.
item.dc:creator: Juraj Bodik, Nikolaj Thams

item.title: Synthetic Data Augmentation for Functional Data: Wasserstein Risk Bounds and Diffusion-Based Conditional Generation
item.description: arXiv:2610.34120v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Functional data are costly to collect; samples of tens to hundreds of curves are common. Synthetic data augmentation can help, but its theory is developed for finite-dimensional data and relies on total variation, which is uninformative for functions. We study augmentation with a class-conditional functional diffusion generator and state guarantees in the Wasserstein-1 distance. For stable downstream estimators, we bound the risk of training on synthetic curves, from above and below, by the risk of training on as many real curves plus a generation penalty, and derive the best number of synthetic curves and a condition under which synthetic data outperform real data. For allocating synthetic curves under class imbalance, we bound the excess risk of training on real and synthetic curves together, without sample splitting. In applications to temperature, hyperspectral and gait curves, augmentation improved classification, function-to-scalar regression and function-to-function regression, and directing synthetic curves to the minority class gave the largest gain under class imbalance.
item.dc:creator: Yuhao Qi, Wenlin Dai, Xuehu Zhu

item.title: Population-average trajectories and slopes in smooth random changepoint mixed models
item.description: arXiv:2610.34165v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Two-slope mixed-effects models with subject-specific changepoints are widely used to describe biphasic longitudinal trajectories. Treatment-arm summaries are often reported using a single "typical subject" curve obtained by plugging mean parameter values into the subject-specific model. This can be misleading when changepoint timing varies across individuals, because averaging subject-specific curves is not the same as evaluating one curve at average parameter values. A related issue is that individual trajectories may bend gradually rather than change slope through a literal kink, with transition sharpness varying between subjects. We propose population-average estimands for two-slope mixed models with random changepoints and smooth subject-level transitions. These estimands target the treatment-arm mean trajectory and instantaneous slope by averaging over fitted heterogeneity in changepoint timing and transition sharpness. We use a baseline-anchored normal-convolution soft hinge, which preserves the broken stick interpretation, includes the abrupt changepoint model as a limiting case, and allows analytic evaluation of the changepoint-marginalized kernels under a truncated normal changepoint distribution for fixed transition sharpness. Averaging over the fitted transition sharpness distribution is then performed by deterministic one-dimensional quadrature. In an application to HIV-1 RNA data from ACTG Protocol 315, with censoring and heavy-tailed residuals, the marginal summaries reveal a more gradual population-level transition than conventional plug-in summaries. The marginal slope remains more negative for longer, and the marginal mean continues to decline after the plug-in curve has begun to flatten. These results illustrate the main reporting implication: in random changepoint models, representative subject curves should not be treated as population-average trajectories or slopes.
item.dc:creator: Divan A. Burger, Sean van der Merwe, Emmanuel Lesaffre

item.title: Conformal Prediction with Stable Measurement Mechanisms
item.description: arXiv:2610.34204v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In applications such as air-quality monitoring, inexpensive sensor readings can help predict pollutant concentrations measured by a separate reference instrument. We study how to adapt conformal prediction intervals to a new population when reference outcomes are available in the source data, but only sensor readings and context, such as weather conditions, are available in the target. We assume that the measurement distribution at a given outcome and context remains stable, while context frequencies and outcome distributions may change. This model is a particular form of causal mechanism shift. Its statistical restriction has been studied as sparse joint shift. Using established marginal matching, predictive adjustment, and weighted conformal calibration, we examine what this restriction contributes to coverage and interval length for continuous outcomes. Gaussian analyses show how measurement stability can identify outcome changes and how retaining context can shorten prediction intervals. For Gaussian models with known source mechanisms, we derive exact coverage formulas in the large-calibration limit while keeping the unlabeled target sample finite. These formulas explain when sharing a correction across contexts is preferable to fitting separate corrections, and why estimating outcome variability is particularly sensitive to weakly informative measurements. Experiments on synthetic Gaussian data show a coverage gain over covariate weighting at the same mean length and a length reduction of about $8\%$ relative to pooled label adjustment at comparable coverage. On the Air Quality dataset, controlled shifts yield coverage gains with longer intervals, while spring-to-autumn and year-over-year transfers show substantial undercoverage.
item.dc:creator: Seungjin Choi

item.title: Pooling interval-monitored step-stress accelerated life tests for reliability prediction: A failure-rate-based meta-analysis for the proportional hazards family
item.description: arXiv:2610.34231v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reliability qualification often relies on several step-stress accelerated life tests conducted in separate campaigns, laboratories, or test rigs, each with its own stress profile, sample size, and inspection schedule, and with units inspected only periodically so that only failure counts between inspections are recorded. Existing meta-analysis methods combine several step-stress experiments but require exactly observed failure times. Methods for interval-inspected step-stress data, on the other hand, have been developed only for a single experiment. This paper develops a failure-rate-based meta-analysis framework for multiple interval-inspected step-stress experiments within the proportional hazards family, linking the experiments through a common underlying lifetime model and a log-linear stress-life relationship. Maximum likelihood estimators and confidence intervals are derived for the model parameters and for engineering quantities of interest at normal operating conditions, including mission reliability, mean time to failure, and lifetime quantiles such as the 0.10 quantile (B10 life). For the LED data, pooling the two tests reduced the RMSE of the estimated reliability at 5 hours by about 20% and that of the 0.10 quantile by about 66%, compared with the better single test. A misspecification study shows that the median is robust to the choice of lifetime distribution (relative bias below 6%), whereas tail quantiles can have a relative bias of up to 34% that does not vanish as the sample size increases, which is critical for warranty decisions. The methodology is illustrated with simulated data and with two step-stress tests of light-emitting diodes.
item.dc:creator: Pranoy Palit, Ayan Pal, Kiran Prajapat

item.title: Nonlinear Reduced-Bias Extreme Value Index Estimators: A Comparative Study
item.description: arXiv:2610.34308v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The estimation of the extreme value index (EVI) plays a central role in extreme value theory (EVT), particularly in the statistical modelling of heavy-tailed phenomena. Classical semi-parametric estimators of the EVI are known to suffer from substantial bias, especially for moderate sample sizes and for common choices of the number of upper order statistics. In recent years, several reduced-bias (RB) methodologies have been proposed in order to improve finite-sample performance while preserving asymptotic efficiency. In this paper, we present new classes of nonlinear RB EVI-estimators based on power mean-type and Lehmer mean-type functionals of upper log-excesses. Under a unified higher-order framework, asymptotic representations are derived and bias and variance properties are compared relative to other RB EVI classes introduced in the literature. An asymptotic comparison at optimal levels is conducted to identify regions of the space parameter where the proposed estimators are more efficient. A comprehensive Monte Carlo simulation study assesses the finite sample behaviour of the new estimators for several heavy tailed models. The results show that nonlinear reduced-bias estimators can provide improvements in bias and root mean squared error, although their relative performance depends on the underlying distribution and the choice of the tuning parameter. An application to hydrological data illustrates their practical use and the importance of threshold selection in EVI estimation.
item.dc:creator: L\'igia Henriques-Rodrigues, Frederico Caeiro, M. Ivette Gomes

item.title: Complete Cancer Prevalence Predictions via LASSO Regularization and Flexible Parametric Survival Cure Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.34314v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cancer prevalence is a key measure of disease burden, and accurate projections are essential for healthcare planning and resource allocation. The Prevalence Incidence Analysis Model (PIAMOD) is widely used to estimate and project cancer prevalence in population-based studies by combining incidence rates and net survival within a forward calculation framework. We propose an improved approach to projecting cancer prevalence by using regularization techniques to select the optimal incidence model and flexible parametric survival cure models to improve the estimation of net survival. The proposed and conventional approaches were compared through a simulation study and an application to population-based data on patients diagnosed with colon cancer in Sweden between 1958 and 2019. Applying the proposed methodology, colon cancer prevalence in Sweden was projected through 2030. The number of individuals living with a previous diagnosis of colon cancer is projected to continue increasing, reaching approximately 550 per 100\,000 males and 500 per 100\,000 females by 2030. Careful model selection is essential when estimating measures of disease burden such as cancer prevalence. The projected increase in colon cancer prevalence in Sweden reflects continued improvements in survival for both sexes and highlights the growing number of individuals living with colon cancer.
item.dc:creator: Fabrizio Di Mari, Roberta De Angelis, Therese ML Andersson, Enoch Yi-Tung Chen, Silvia Rossi, Paul W Dickman, Roberto Rocci, Mark Clements

item.title: Inference for Causal Path-Specific Effects in Longitudinal Studies with Repeated Treatments and Multiple Mediators
item.description: arXiv:2610.34349v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In longitudinal studies, repeated treatments may be followed by different sequences of mediators and time-varying covariates. We develop semiparametric inference for path-specific effects in this setting, allowing the number, type, and ordering of intermediate variables to vary across treatment occasions. Under consistency, positivity, edge consistency, and the cross-world restrictions of a nonparametric structural equation model with independent errors, path-specific means are identified by the edge g-formula. We derive two parameterizations of the efficient influence function of the identifying functional. The first follows the observed-data factorization and uses conditional intermediate-variable densities. The second uses sequential regressions to replace the corresponding integrations and Bayes' rule to express density ratios through treatment-history regressions, thereby avoiding direct estimation of intermediate-variable densities. Each yields a one-step estimator that permits flexible nuisance estimation. We establish product-rate conditions for asymptotic linearity and semiparametric efficiency. The density-based estimator has blockwise multiple robustness, generalizing triply robust estimation, while the regression-based estimator has sequential multiple robustness. We further develop a sensitivity analysis for selected violations of cross-world independence assumptions used to identify these effects. Simulations examine finite-sample performance and robustness to model misspecifications. An application to the Framingham Heart Study examines sustained-smoking effects on systolic blood pressure along pathways through repeated body mass index measurements. The proposed methods are implemented in the R package flexPaths on Gihub at xxou/flexPaths.
item.dc:creator: Xiaxian Ou, Xinwei He, Razieh Nabi

item.title: Post-Progression Treatment Regimes and the Limits of Cross-Trial Survival Transport
item.description: arXiv:2610.34513v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Models transporting overall survival (OS) effects across clinical trials fail when they ignore the "post-progression treatment regime"---the subsequent therapy rates across biomarker strata and randomized arms. Because this trial-level regime is systematically omitted from published reports, standard correction families are structurally inadequate: crossover adjustments target an unrealistic counterfactual with zero subsequent therapy, erasing critical environmental differences; population adjustments (including MAIC, STC, AIPW, and density ratios) match baseline individual covariates, leaving trial-level regimes mismatched. We show that these correction approaches carry near-identical bias, proving the failure is informational rather than methodological. Simulations demonstrate that ignoring the target setting's landscape can leave the directional sign of the transported effect completely undetermined, even when mechanisms are fully known. Conversely, providing the target regime to a regime-aware estimator successfully recovers the true treatment effect. Code is available at https://github.com/felizzi/post-progression-transport-WMHS-NeurIPS-2026.
item.dc:creator: Federico Felizzi, Noman Paracha

item.title: Demand Estimation with Unobserved Stockout Substitution: Exact Likelihood Maximization
item.description: arXiv:2610.34547v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When a product is sold out, customers who prefer it may buy a substitute or leave without purchasing. Efficient demand estimation in this setting is challenging when inventory is observed only at replenishments, because the stockout times, and hence the products available to each customer, are unobserved. Estimating demand efficiently under stockout substitution has been a challenging problem since Anupindi et al. (1998), and it has become more pressing as the scale of such problem instances grows thanks to innovations in retailing such as unmanned stores. We provide a complete solution to this problem for the multinomial logit (MNL) model, the most widely used model of customer choice. Using a continuous-time representation of the purchase process developed in Zhou et al. (2026), we show that the exact likelihood and its gradient are one-dimensional integrals, no matter how many products, customers, or stockouts there are. Both can be evaluated at a cost linear in the numbers of products and periods. Our method estimates demand for 2,000 products from 2,000 selling periods in under ten minutes.
item.dc:creator: Chenhao Wang, Hansheng Jiang, Ningyuan Chen

item.title: Flexible Estimation of Covariate-Specific Win Ratio for Prioritized Time-to-Event Outcomes
item.description: arXiv:2610.34567v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prioritized time-to-event outcomes arise frequently in clinical studies, where treatment comparisons may be based on a prespecified hierarchy of clinically important outcomes. The win ratio provides a natural summary of treatment benefit for such prioritized outcomes. However, methods for characterizing heterogeneous treatment effects by estimating how the win ratio varies with baseline covariates remain limited in this setting. We develop a flexible local inverse probability of censoring weighted estimator of the win ratio as a function of baseline covariates, without imposing the parametric shape or proportional win-fractions structure assumed by existing regression approaches. We use best linear projections to summarize the estimated log win ratio and develop formal tests of log-linearity of the win ratio function. We also propose a complementary model-based estimator of the covariate-specific win ratio assuming proportional hazards models for the marginal distributions, copula dependence between the margins, and Bernstein-polynomial sieves for the baseline hazards. Large-sample properties and bootstrap validity are established for both approaches. Simulations show that the local estimator is robust, while the model-based procedure can provide substantial efficiency and power gains under correct specification, and proportional win-fractions regression may lead to bias when its structural assumptions fail. The methods are illustrated by analyzing data from CALGB 9633, a randomized lung cancer trial.
item.dc:creator: Zhiguo Li, Xiaofei Wang

item.title: Towards the Revival of Survival Ratio
item.description: arXiv:2610.34619v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The hazard ratio is the most commonly reported measure in survival analysis, yet it suffers from well-documented limitations, including non-collapsibility and susceptibility to selection bias as treatment-specific risk sets change over time. In this article, we revisit the survival ratio and the cumulative incidence ratio as alternative measures that directly compare survival and failure probabilities. We introduce a novel modeling framework that targets these ratio functions and constructs coherent nuisance models so that the target and nuisance parameters are variation independent. The framework yields valid monotone survival and cumulative distribution functions and supports likelihood-based and doubly robust estimation of the target parameters, together with estimation of covariate-specific survival and cumulative incidence curves. We illustrate the proposed frameworks using two clinical-trial datasets. In a prostate cancer trial, the estimated survival ratio for 1.0 mg estrogen versus placebo increased over follow-up, while a descriptive selected-cohort analysis of a breast cancer screening trial yielded a cumulative incidence ratio that crossed one over time.
item.dc:creator: Ruixuan Zhao, Jingxin Yan, Xiaochuan Shi, Torben Martinussen, Eric Tchetgen Tchetgen, Linbo Wang

item.title: Calibration of robust covariance estimation under heavy tails
item.description: arXiv:2610.34622v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Minimum Covariance Determinant (MCD) estimator is one of the most widely used high-breakdown estimators of multivariate location and scatter. Its practical success relies on suitable corrections, which remove the asymptotic and small-sample biases introduced by trimming. While explicit consistency factors are available under the multivariate normal distribution and, more recently, under multivariate Student-t models, these corrections only address the asymptotic behavior of the estimator. In the Gaussian case, it is known showed that the MCD also exhibits a non-negligible finite-sample bias, particularly for small sample sizes and relatively large dimensions. Such bias propagates to robust Mahalanobis distances and may affect subsequent procedures, including multivariate outlier detection and robust inference. This paper investigates the finite-sample behavior of the MCD estimator and of the related robust distances under multivariate Student-t distributions, a potentially relevant scenario in many application fields. Extensive Monte Carlo experiments are carried out over a broad range of sample sizes, dimensions, trimming levels and degrees of freedom. Based on these experiments, empirical correction factors are obtained and approximated by smooth functions, providing a computationally efficient calibration suitable for practical implementations to heavy-tailed data. The proposed corrections are developed both for the scatter bias and the robust distance quantiles, thus leading to improved approximations for robust inference.
item.dc:creator: Andrea Cerioli, Domenico Perrotta, Francesca Torti

item.title: The Effect of Residual Confounding in the Analysis of Large Observational Data Sets
item.description: arXiv:2610.34648v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We review how residual confounding in large observational data sets can mistakenly lead researchers to declare a predictor variable statistically significant. As sample sizes become very large, standard errors decrease dramatically, causing unmeasured variables correlated with the predictor of interest to overwhelm the model and yield precise estimates of the wrong thing, the residual confounder. Three examples from environmental epidemiology are provided. Specification Curve Analysis, SCA, and Local Control Analysis, LCA, are offered to reveal model selection bias and true null effects.
item.dc:creator: S. Stanley Young, Warren B. Kindzierski

item.title: Pro-Active Inference
item.description: arXiv:2610.34681v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Estimating a population mean is fundamental across scientific applications, but observing every outcome can be prohibitively expensive. Often, covariates and machine learning (ML) predictions are available for the full population, even when only a small subset of outcomes can be observed. How can we leverage this information to proactively select observations to label, update ML predictions as labels arrive, and construct statistically valid confidence intervals? We develop a general, without-replacement formulation of Pro-Active Inference (PAI), extending our earlier with-replacement approach and building on Active Statistical Inference. Rather than making fixed-order label-skip decisions, PAI proactively selects which observation to label next from the remaining covariate pool while accommodating online ML updates. We establish PAI's finite-sample unbiasedness and asymptotic validity, develop an improved finite-sample variance estimator, and extend PAI to superpopulation inference without Bonferroni corrections or $\alpha$-splitting. We characterize PAI's potential efficiency gains over Batch Active Inference in a quasi-oracle setting, highlighting the role of prediction-residual imbalance. Across eight diverse datasets, PAI achieves greater sampling efficiency than Sequential Active Inference in the vast majority of tested settings with near-nominal statistical coverage, using the same ML predictor and uncertainty score. However, comparisons with simpler baselines such as Prediction-Powered Inference and uniform sampling, as well as the closely related Prediction-Powered Active Testing, reveal when additional adaptivity helps or hurts statistical efficiency. Through interpretable, theory-motivated diagnostics and frozen-ML ablations, we investigate when and why PAI gains or loses efficiency, highlighting the initial residual-estimation problem and subsequent online learning dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Skyler Wu, Yash Nair, Antoine Maechler, Emmanuel J. Cand\`es

item.title: Designing Customer Feedback for Subscription Boxes
item.description: arXiv:2610.34726v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Problem definition: Subscription box services often ask customers for ratings before choosing what to send. Responses are scarce, and longer questionnaires and finer scales lower completion. We study which candidate items a questionnaire should ask about, and in what format, when the platform then selects a fixed number of them. A design is judged by the expected value lost by not selecting the truly best items. Methodology/results: We approximate each ordinal rating by a Gaussian signal carrying its information at the cutoff between selected and unselected items. As equal numbers of responses per item grow, the ratio of this proxy's loss to the exact loss tends to one. With 1 to 100 responses per item, the two are within about 7 percent. Averaging the information over the prior instead can misstate the loss by about half. For an item far from the cutoff, the value of responses grows slowly at first and then faster, so our envelope rule values responses in blocks. In simulations with a correct prior it lowers the loss by 15 to 81 percent relative to an even spread, and on MovieLens ratings by 6 to 25 percent. Under the proxy, with responses allocated optimally, formats are ranked exactly by one number, the expected information per customer asked. Choosing the format this way comes within about 2 percent of the best on average. Managerial implications: Feedback should go to items whose place in the selection is unclear. Planning helps most when the platform's prior beliefs are informative and right. A platform unsure of its prior should widen it and send the questionnaire in waves. Calibrated on MovieLens ratings, a five-point answer carries about 1.7 times the information of a like/dislike answer, so at equal length the finer scale is better when it cuts completion by less than about 40 percent.
item.dc:creator: Renjun Hu, Hyun-Soo Ahn, Stefanus Jasin

item.title: Multivariate Augmented Prediction-Powered Survival Inference for EHR Association Studies With Limited Chart Review
item.description: arXiv:2610.34749v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Objective: To reduce bias and improve precision in survival association studies using electronic health record (EHR) data when computational phenotypes (CPs) for outcomes and covariates are error-prone and chart review is limited. Materials and Methods: We developed Multivariate Augmented Prediction-Powered Survival (MAPS) regression, which combines chart-reviewed and CP-derived labels across different validation patterns. MAPS uses a discrete-time survival model with a complementary log-log link to estimate hazard ratios (HRs). It incorporates data-adaptive augmentation weights, inverse-probability sampling weights, and patient-level cluster-robust variance estimation. We compared MAPS with chart-reviewed data (CRD) and CP-only analyses in simulation studies and a masked-validation study of immune-related adverse events (irAEs) among 1,026 patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors. Results: In the main simulations, MAPS produced approximately unbiased estimates and generally near-nominal 95% confidence interval (CI) coverage, with narrower intervals than CRD. CP-only estimates became increasingly biased as CP errors increased. In the EHR analysis, MAPS estimates closely agreed with fully validated estimates and improved precision over CRD, particularly at lower validation rates. CP-only analysis suggested increased irAE risk associated with pre-existing autoimmune disease (AID; HR=1.53; 95% CI, 1.12-2.09), whereas the fully validated analysis did not (HR=0.93; 95% CI, 0.67-1.29). Discussion: Precision gains depended on CP quality and validation rates, while small validation samples may affect confidence interval coverage. Conclusion: MAPS provides a flexible and efficient approach to EHR-based survival inference by combining limited chart-reviewed data with error-prone CPs across different validation patterns.
item.dc:creator: Xicheng Xie, Katherine Fiona Simpson, Hyojung Jang, Theresa L. Walunas, Lili Zhao

item.title: Adaptive Probe Design for Auditing AI Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.34751v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How can we audit an AI agent before it is safe and practical to deploy? A central task is to estimate its performance under the intended deployment policy (the target policy). However, historical observations may provide insufficient coverage of relevant states and actions, limiting evaluation reliability. We propose CAD (Flow-Constrained Audit Design), a framework that combines historical logs with a limited budget of targeted audit trials (probes). The key idea is to design probes that minimize the mismatch between the combined state-action visitation distribution (occupancy) of the logs and probes and that of the target policy. We formulate this design as a constrained convex optimization problem, directing probes toward regions important to the target policy but underrepresented in historical logs. We develop an adaptive algorithm that iteratively estimates environment dynamics and occupancies to update the probe policy. We link occupancy mismatch to bounds on mean squared error and asymptotic variance, and establish error bounds for CAD's adaptive estimator in finite and continuous state spaces. Experiments in Gridworld, LunarLander, and autonomous driving using real-world logs from the Waymo Open Motion Dataset show improved estimation accuracy over alternative data collection and probe designs.
item.dc:creator: Zhenghan Li, Xuan Bi, Jie Ding

item.title: A new categorical correlation measure
item.description: arXiv:2610.34932v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Feature screening in high-dimensional classification is an important problem in statistical learning, particularly in genomics, imaging, and other scientific fields, especially when the number of predictors exceeds the sample size. Zhong et al. (2024) present a semi-distance covariance (SDCov) as a dependence measure between a categorical random variable and a multivariate continuous random vector, presenting it as a promising tool for group-wise feature screening. However, SDCov is defined using the Euclidean norm, and its performance may be affected when the data is derived from heavy-tailed distributions or when outlier observations are present, which is a common phenomenon in high-dimensional data. This study proposes a modification of SDCov by replacing the $L_2$ norm with an $L_1$ norm. This adjustment results in a dependency measure between a categorical variable and a multivariate continuous variable that maintains the independence-characterization property of the original definition. Additionally, it serves as a robust and interpretable measure, particularly in the presence of outliers in the data. We establish the fundamental theoretical properties of the proposed measure and introduce a U-statistics-based estimator along with JEL-based inference for the measure. Additionally, we have introduced a test for independence based on the proposed measure. An extensive Monte Carlo simulation is performed to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed measure in comparison to existing measures in the literature. The proposed measure is applied in feature screening, as illustrated with the ADNI Alzheimer's disease dataset and the Iris dataset. The data analysis shows the proposed measure's effectiveness in identifying variables that facilitate strong class separation of the respective response variables.
item.dc:creator: Saparya Suresh, Sudheesh K. Kattumannil, Sujit Ghosh

item.title: Breakdown-Resistant Hierarchical Bayesian Calibration for Multi-Center Clinical Trials
item.description: arXiv:2610.34997v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-center clinical trials are threatened by systematic location shifts in biomarkers measured across devices, sites, or reagent batches. Hierarchical Bayesian models are the standard remedy, borrowing strength across centers by pooling center-specific estimates. However, we prove that the standard Gaussian hierarchical posterior has a breakdown point of zero \emph{at the level of the posterior distribution itself}: a single contaminated center drives the posterior mean of every clean center to infinity and collapses the coverage of every clean center's credible interval to zero. We introduce the Posterior-Median Hierarchical Calibration (PMHC) framework, a fully Bayesian hierarchical model that replaces the Gaussian prior on center-specific shifts with a Laplace prior. Under absolute loss, the posterior median is the natural Bayes estimator, and we prove that its breakdown point is $\lfloor (K+1)/2 \rfloor$ contaminated centers---whereas the Gaussian posterior mean has breakdown point zero for every $K$. PMHC retains a full posterior distribution, enabling meaningful credible intervals and posterior probabilities. Across $K \in \{5, 10, 20\}$ centers and $n \in \{50, 200, 1000\}$ observations per center, PMHC maintains $94$--$98\%$ coverage under contamination fraction $\epsilon = 0.60$, while Gaussian pooling collapses to $0.0\%$ coverage and its point estimate diverges by a factor of $54$. On real NHANES data ($n = 60{,}651$ across nine cycles), contamination in three cycles collapsed the Gaussian coverage to \(0.0\%\) and shifted clean cycles by \(0.41\) mg/dL, whereas PMHC maintained \(94.0\%\) coverage with a shift of \(0.008\) mg/dL. To our knowledge, this is the first explicit breakdown analysis of the \emph{posterior distribution} in hierarchical Bayesian pooling, and the first Bayesian model that is simultaneously contamination-robust and efficient in the clean-data regime.
item.dc:creator: Safaa K. Kadhem

item.title: Conformal Novelty Detection via Data-enhanced Localization
item.description: arXiv:2610.34999v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Novelty detection is an important area of research in both statistics and machine learning. In this paper, we focus on the conditional novelty detection problem, where novelties arise from the relationship between different variables. We first adopt the conformal inference framework and propose a data-enhanced localized conformal p-value, constructed by recalibrating an enhanced conditional distribution estimator. This estimator efficiently captures conditional information by incorporating both calibration and test data into its kernel estimation. We show that our p-values are valid in finite samples and can improve detection efficiency. Based on this p-value, we then develop a novel conditional novelty detection algorithm, along with a data-driven bandwidth selection method that ensures finite-sample false discovery rate control while enhancing detection power. Both simulated and real data experiments demonstrate the advantages of our proposed approach.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoyang Wu, Jiajun Liu, Haojie Ren, Changliang Zou

item.title: Fast Calibration of Generalized Posteriors via Dirichlet Reweighting
item.description: arXiv:2610.35187v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While generalized Bayesian inference offers a principled approach to uncertainty quantification under general loss functions, its practical performance depends critically on the choice of the learning rate. Generalized posterior calibration, which selects the learning rate so that the resulting credible sets attain nominal frequentist coverage, is computationally intensive because it relies on repeated posterior sampling across bootstrap datasets and candidate learning rates. To overcome this practical difficulty, we propose a fast calibration method that combines Dirichlet-weighted bootstrap perturbations with importance sampling to estimate coverage while reducing the need for repeated posterior sampling. We further extend the framework to hierarchical models, where group-specific learning rates are calibrated and stabilized via shrinkage. Illustrative examples using quantile regression, support vector machines, and hierarchical Huber regression demonstrate that the proposed method substantially reduces computational cost while maintaining accurate calibration.
item.dc:creator: Shonosuke Sugasawa

item.title: Comparing Measurements of Pictorial Depth: Conditions for Placing Methods, Observers and Depiction Styles on One Scale
item.description: arXiv:2610.35200v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Two observers can agree about what lies in front in a picture yet report different amounts of apparent depth. People report pictorial depth by judging which of two points looks nearer, setting a probe to match a surface, adjusting relative sizes, or rating three-dimensionality. Two such methods can agree closely without sharing a unit. We ask when different methods, observers, depiction styles and viewing conditions can share one scale. Each set of scores, a measurement block, is a graph node. Two blocks are linked only if their shared observations pass six checks fixed in advance, among them outcome type, removal of declared offsets and position effects, proportionality and covariance. If the adjusted shared patterns are exactly proportional, a connected graph fixes every block's gain, its relative scale factor. The checks accept proportionality only within a set margin, so a link supports the gains without proving exact proportionality. One unit is still not one depth coordinate. Suppose each block scores shared stimuli with its own origin and positive unit. A matrix-rank test then decides when a common coordinate is identified: when only one overall origin and unit remain free. If each shared stimulus, an anchor, is scored by exactly two blocks, this needs two disjoint sets of anchors, each connecting every block, their compatibility assumed, not tested. They also suffice, except for anchor values satisfying exact polynomial relations (probability zero for anchor values drawn from any distribution with a density). We adapt network gain estimation from test linking, with a loop-consistency check. A reanalysis of published probe settings on 3-D renderings passes one of 171 candidate depiction-style links through all six checks, each judged by its own 95% bound, unadjusted for the 171 pairs. Links between tasks remain untested; they need shared stimuli and a joint uncertainty model.
item.dc:creator: Adam Y. Shavit

item.title: Byzantine-Robust Sparse Regression with Missing Covariates
item.description: arXiv:2610.35321v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study distributed sparse linear regression with missing covariates and Byzantine workers. Correcting for missing observations can make the regression loss nonconvex, while Byzantine reports can distort gradient updates and impair estimation. A communication-efficient method is proposed that combines robust gradient aggregation with folded-concave regularization. Under appropriate regularity conditions, after $t$ communication rounds the estimation error is bounded by a transient component determined by the initial error and decaying geometrically with $t$, plus a residual component reflecting finite-sample variability and Byzantine contamination. Simulations and two real-data examples evaluate estimation accuracy, variable selection, and communication costs.
item.dc:creator: Xiaofei Wu, Rongmei Liang, Jian Qing Shi

item.title: Homogeneity Pursuit for 3D Point Clouds
item.description: arXiv:2610.35417v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper proposes a novel classification learning approach to identify the latent group structures in 3D point clouds collected with irregular shapes, which allows 3D point clouds to be classified into different groups with the number of groups and the group membership unknown. 3D point clouds within a group have a common mean function, while mean function heterogeneity is allowed across groups. We first obtain preliminary estimates of the individual mean functions by penalized trivariate splines over triangulation. Based on these preliminary estimates, we develop an agglomerative clustering algorithm to estimate the unknown group structures and propose a ratio criterion to determine the number of groups. We establish the consistency of the estimated number of groups and group membership. Furthermore, we investigate a post-grouping trivariate penalized spline estimation procedure for group-specific mean functions and derive the corresponding asymptotic theory. The proposed method is validated through simulation studies and showcased with an application to the imaging data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative database.
item.dc:creator: Haojie Dong, Hanbing Zhu, Xinghui Wang, Xuejun Wang, Xinyuan Song

item.title: Distribution-free predictive inference with instrumental variables
item.description: arXiv:2610.35605v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the problem of predictive inference with outcomes missing not at random, when instrumental variables are available. While conformal prediction and weighted conformal prediction provide valid distribution-free inference when outcomes are missing completely at random and missing at random, respectively, inference is generally not possible without additional assumptions when outcomes are missing not at random. In this work, we consider a setting where we remain within the distribution-free framework but instead have access to an instrumental variable (IV). We explore the theoretical possibility of IV predictive inference and establish that it is characterized by a parameter that we refer to as the identification index. We derive an impossibility result for the case where the identification index is not sufficiently large, showing that any distribution-free approach fails to provide informative inference in this case. For the case where the identification index is sufficiently large, we introduce a practical method that achieves informative predictive inference. Our method leverages modern semiparametric efficiency theory which involves deriving the efficient influence function of the identifying functional for sharp IV bounds of the quantiles of the missing outcome, delivering a double robustness property in the coverage guarantee of the proposed framework for IV-based predictive inference. We illustrate the theoretical results and the performance of the proposed procedure through simulations and two real-data applications---FES wages and NHANES III self-reported heights.
item.dc:creator: Yonghoon Lee, Edgar Dobriban, Eric Tchetgen Tchetgen

item.title: Estimating Treatment Effects in Complex Disease Dynamics: Immortal Time, Varying Hazards, and Multiple Time Scales
item.description: arXiv:2610.35678v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In observational survival studies, delayed treatment initiation can induce immortal time bias in effect estimation when treatment groups are defined by future uptake. Despite originating from distinct predictive or causal inference paradigms, time-dependent approaches (e.g. the time-dependent Cox model, landmark supermodel, multi-state model, and g-formula) are often treated as interchangeable in applied research when addressing immortal time bias. These models effectively reclassify person-time according to time-varying exposure, yet the interpretation of their target estimands depends on assumptions about the underlying disease process and clinically relevant time scales. We study effect estimation for allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation under baseline intention-to-transplant strategies in acute myeloid leukemia (i.e. transplantation is planned for a prespecified time, subject to the patient's eligibility), within a multi-state framework allowing time-inhomogeneous Markov, semi-Markov, and state arrival extended semi-Markov dynamics. Using target trial emulation, we benchmark, on the probability scale, estimates derived from Cox-type time-dependent models and the g-formula against the corresponding theoretical values implied by the stochastic data-generating process. Decomposing the partial likelihood score, we show that single-time-scale models can be systematically biased when death intensities from different originating states are not proportional on a common time scale, as can occur when the clock is reset after intermediate events. We quantify these findings in a phase III simulation study and illustrate their implications in an application to data from three acute myeloid leukemia trials.
item.dc:creator: Yujun Xu, Ulrich Mansmann

item.title: Recertifying decisions via e-closure: uniform improvements of conformal risk control and randomized e-BH
item.description: arXiv:2610.35821v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Statistical procedures often control expected loss at a prescribed level while leaving part of their risk budget unused. Building on the e-value representation of risk-controlled decisions and the e-closure principle for multiple testing, we formulate recertification, a general paradigm for improving procedures by exploiting computable slack in their validity certificates.
